overview: This file documents U.S. State and War Department efforts between August and October 1946 to restore and regulate communications with occupied Japan. One group of papers concerns commercial telegraph traffic routed through the United States between Japan and Pacific military bases, including proposed and final rate schedules for ordinary, code, deferred, night-letter, VLT, and EFM services. A second group proposes allowing censored commercial correspondence between Allied and Japanese firms to stimulate exports while retaining SCAP control over production, contracts, and foreign trade. The papers trace interdepartmental review, successive cable drafts, and the transition from tightly controlled occupation commerce toward freer competitive trade.

subfiles.title: Memorandum from Martin to Hilldring on telecommunications with Pacific bases
subfiles.about: The memorandum seeks approval of a cable authorizing commercial telegraph service through the United States between Japan and specified Pacific military bases.
subfiles.summary: Martin reports that U.S. carriers supplied rates and that Treasury cleared the proposed wording. The attached draft approves service to Papeete, New Caledonia, Suva, and Samoa, with U.S.-to-base rates ranging from ten to thirty cents per word. Messages would pass through San Francisco, and existing Japan–United States rules concerning yen conversion, message classes, and eligible users would remain in force.

subfiles.title: Whitman memorandum proposing commercial mail with Japan
subfiles.about: Whitman proposes using censored commercial correspondence between Allied and Japanese firms to stimulate Japanese exports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum revisits an August proposal after SCAP sought commercial-information telegraph service and the United States recommended commercial-information mail. Its draft cable proposes a blanket Trading with the Enemy Act exemption for non-transactional correspondence about approved exports, while preserving censorship and the exclusion of objectionable firms. Private exchanges, including samples, would produce tentative agreements, but importers would submit dollar offers through USCC and final transactions would remain subject to SCAP control. If SCAP approved the principle, the United States would seek prompt FEC approval.

subfiles.title: Easton routing note returning commercial-mail papers
subfiles.about: Easton returns material to Whitman in response to a request.
subfiles.summary: This brief Division of Defense Materials routing note records the return of the commercial-mail material from Easton to Whitman. The central line is badly corrupted by OCR but evidently states that the papers were returned as requested; the sheet bears a September 3, 1946 stamp.

subfiles.title: Socks memorandum returning the proposed commercial-mail cable
subfiles.from: Lieutenant Colonel Hugh G. Socks, Acting Executive, CAD
subfiles.about: Socks returns the proposed cable on commercial mail with Japan following a telephone conversation with Lieutenant Colonel Dice.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Executive of the Civil Affairs Division states that the proposed cable is being returned at Easton's request. The action followed a telephone conversation with Lieutenant Colonel Dice on the same date.

subfiles.title: Draft cable to SCAP on commercial mail and export promotion
subfiles.about: The draft asks SCAP to consider permitting controlled commercial correspondence between Allied and Japanese firms as a means of expanding exports.
subfiles.summary: The draft proposes a Trading with the Enemy Act exemption for non-transactional correspondence concerning commodities on the approved export program. Mail would be censored, objectionable firms could be excluded, and exchanges of messages and samples could establish tentative production and purchase agreements involving Boeki Cho. U.S. importers would pass dollar offers to USCC, while SCAP would decide whether proposed transactions made suitable use of Japanese resources and offered satisfactory prices. The proposal is presented as a way to place preliminary negotiations in private hands and ease the transition to competitive trade.

subfiles.title: Outgoing War Department message on VLT and EFM services
subfiles.about: The message reports where VLT and EFM services from Japan are available and supplies the applicable message and per-word rates.
subfiles.summary: RCA Communications and Mackay confirm that VLT and EFM services are unavailable between Japan and New Caledonia, Papeete, Samoa, and Suva. Both services are available to Alaska, Guam, Midway, Honolulu, Puerto Rico, Saint Thomas, and the Canal Zone, with EFM priced at sixty cents per message and VLT charged at the night-letter word rate with a ten-word minimum. The telegram provides full, code, deferred, and night-letter rates for each destination and was handled as restricted correspondence.

subfiles.title: O'Sullivan memorandum requesting concurrence in Pacific-islands cable
subfiles.to: Colonel R. H. Chard, Executive Officer, CAD
subfiles.about: O'Sullivan asks the Civil Affairs Division to report War Department concurrence or requested changes to an attached cable for SCAP.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum transmits a State Department draft cable concerning telecommunications with Pacific islands. O'Sullivan requests prompt notice of War Department concurrence or any desired revisions. A handwritten notation indicates that CAD was notified of A-H concurrence on October 16.

subfiles.title: Routed draft cable to SCAP on telecommunications rates
subfiles.about: This routed draft reports the availability and rates of VLT and EFM service between Japan and several U.S. or Pacific destinations.
subfiles.summary: The draft states that VLT and EFM service is unavailable to New Caledonia, Papeete, Samoa, and Suva but available to Alaska, Guam, Midway, Honolulu, Puerto Rico, Saint Thomas, and the Canal Zone. It supplies a sixty-cent EFM message charge and destination-specific VLT composition rates. The OCR date of 1967 is an evident error for 1946, given the surrounding papers and routing context.

subfiles.title: Clean draft cable from War to SCAP on VLT and EFM service
subfiles.about: The draft provides service-availability findings and detailed rates for VLT and EFM traffic originating in Japan.
subfiles.summary: RCA Communications and Mackay are said to have confirmed that VLT and EFM services do not reach New Caledonia, Papeete, Samoa, or Suva from Japan. The services are available to seven other destinations, with EFM charged per message and VLT at night-letter rates. The draft lists full, code, deferred, and night-letter charges and bears W. L. Cansler's drafting notation.

subfiles.title: Annotated duplicate draft cable from War to SCAP
subfiles.about: This annotated duplicate repeats the proposed VLT and EFM service and rate information for Japan's communications with Pacific and U.S. destinations.
subfiles.summary: The text duplicates the October 10 draft, distinguishing destinations without VLT or EFM service from those where both services were available. It repeats the per-message EFM charge and the full, code, deferred, and night-letter rates. Added routing marks associate the copy with A-H, JK, and O'Sullivan.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how the occupation authorities connected communications policy to Japan's economic recovery: censorship and centralized approval were retained even as officials explored private commercial correspondence and competitive trade. Its successive drafts expose the administrative path among State, War, Treasury, SCAP, SWNCC, and the FEC. The detailed tariff schedules are unusually concrete evidence of the geography and cost of postwar communications, while discrepancies between draft and final rates—notably for Alaska, Puerto Rico, Saint Thomas, and the Canal Zone—allow historians to trace revisions during interdepartmental review.
